tagline: Into a fork: **everything**. Into a subagent: **only the prompt**. Back out of either: **only the final message**.
summary: Forks and subagents differ in what flows **in**, but they are identical in what flows **out**. A fork starts with a **full copy of the parent's context**; a subagent starts with **its agent definition plus the prompt** and nothing else. In both cases, the only thing that ever crosses back to the parent is the child's **final message** — never its transcript, never its tool outputs, never its context.

sections.heading: Inbound: what the child starts with
body: A **fork** begins life as a copy of its parent: same system prompt, same conversation history, same accumulated tool results. The prompt you pass it is **one more instruction on top of everything it already knows**.

A **subagent** begins from its **agent definition** — the system prompt and tool list configured for that agent type — plus the prompt you pass. The parent's conversation **does not exist** for it. If the subagent needs a file path, a constraint, or a decision the parent made, that information must be **written into the prompt**.

sections.heading: Outbound: what the parent gets back
body: Both kinds of child return exactly one thing: their **final message**, delivered to the parent as a **tool result**. The child's tool calls, intermediate reasoning, file reads, and errors stay in the **child's context** and are discarded with it.
This is a feature, not a limitation: it's what makes delegation **context-cheap**. A fork can read fifty files and the parent's context grows by **one message** — the conclusion.

sections.heading: What never crosses (in either direction)
body: The child's **transcript** is not appended to the parent's. The parent's **later turns** do not stream into a running child. And nothing the child does is **shown to the user directly** — the parent decides what to relay.
The one deliberate exception: a finished agent can be **continued by name or ID**, which reopens **its own** preserved context for follow-up — still without merging anything into the parent.

diagram.caption: The boundary is asymmetric: **inbound** differs by child kind, **outbound** is the same minimal channel for both.

nodes.label: Parent context
nodes.note: System prompt + full conversation + accumulated tool results. The parent's working memory.

nodes.label: Spawn: fork or subagent?
nodes.note: The **subagent_type** parameter picks the inbound rule: copy everything, or start clean.

nodes.label: Fork: full copy
nodes.note: The fork's context **starts as a copy of the parent's** — then grows independently as the fork works.

nodes.label: Subagent: definition + prompt
nodes.note: The subagent's context starts with **its own system prompt** and **the prompt it was passed**. Nothing of the parent's conversation.

nodes.label: Child works in its own context
nodes.note: Every tool call, file read, and intermediate step accumulates in the **child's** context window — invisible to the parent.

nodes.label: Final message crosses back
nodes.note: The **only** thing the parent receives. One message, delivered as a tool result. The child's context is not merged back.

scenarios.title: Trace the boundary for a **fork**
scenarios.note: Inbound: **everything** (a copy). Outbound: **one message**. The fork's fifty file-reads cost the parent nothing.

scenarios.title: Trace the boundary for a **subagent**
scenarios.note: Inbound: **only the prompt** — anything the subagent needs to know must be written into it. Outbound: the same **one message**.

misconceptions.myth: The parent can see what its subagent did — the transcript comes back with the result.
misconceptions.reality: Only the **final message** returns. The subagent's transcript, tool outputs, and reasoning are **never** delivered to the parent.
misconceptions.why: It feels like the work should be auditable from the parent. It is auditable — but in the child's own session log, not in the parent's context.

misconceptions.myth: A subagent can look things up in the parent's conversation if it needs to.
misconceptions.reality: A subagent has **no access** to the parent's conversation, before or during its run. If it wasn't in the prompt, the subagent doesn't know it.
misconceptions.why: Forks DO get the parent's conversation, so it's natural to assume subagents do too. The inbound rule is exactly what differs between them.

misconceptions.myth: When a fork finishes, its findings are merged back into the parent's context.
misconceptions.reality: Nothing merges. The parent gets the fork's **final message** as a tool result and decides what to do with it — that's the entire hand-off.
misconceptions.why: 'Fork' suggests an eventual 'join'. There is a join, but it's one message wide.
